props.headline: What each review came back as

beats.narration: In Chapter 10, the error that worried me most is one word. The chapter says APR-246 with azacitidine significantly improved remission in a phase three trial. I went to the trial registry. The trial missed its main goal. Remission was 33.3 percent against 22.4, with a P value of 0.13. Higher, yes. Significant, no. A student reading that sentence would never know.

resolver.label: MISSED ITS PRIMARY ENDPOINT
resolver.detail: The trial completed with results posted. Higher is not the same as significant.

beats.narration: Chapter 13 gave me the strangest error of the whole project. It lists Sticker's sarcoma as a human cancer. It is a cancer of dogs. It also says several drugs that block MMP enzymes are in clinical trials. I searched the registry for 29 drug names and classes and found no active cancer trial. A zero only means something if the search works, so I ran the same search for pembrolizumab and got 1,292.

beats.new_visual_element: Three bars: eleven files, eight with copied runs, five roughly half copied
beats.narration: Parts of Chapter 13 read like other books, so I checked. I compared it against the NCBI Bookshelf chapters it resembled, looking for runs of ten or more identical words. I found 2,140 copied words from 16 Bookshelf chapters, in 8 of its 11 files. And one error came in with the copy: a protein placed on the wrong cells, in a passage lifted word for word.

beats.narration: That copying explained the oddest thing I found. One sentence about spread through the lymph system appears twice. In file 5, under the lung heading, it is correct, because that is the context it was copied from. In file 9 it is wrong. The audit had graded the two copies the wrong way round.

beats.new_visual_element: What passed every check, and what still needed fixing
beats.narration: Then I turned on my own work. In Chapter 10, my eight edits passed every mechanical check I had, and two of them still read badly when I said them out loud. In Chapter 13, I checked my 24 replacement sentences as if someone else had written them. I found four problems, including an and where my source said or, and claims my own sources did not support.

beats.narration: What I took from these two chapters is practical. When text is copied, its mistakes come with it. One word like significant can carry a false claim. And my corrections get the same scrutiny as the chapter does. Both chapters' corrections are now merged into the textbook.
